claim: NompC is a mechanosensitive ion channel responsible for the sensation of touch and balance in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: NompC is a mechanosensitive ion channel responsible for the sensation of touch and balance in Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: NompC can be opened by compression of the intracellular ankyrin repeat domain but not by a stretch.
source: Our results showed that NompC could be opened by compression of the intracellular ankyrin repeat domain but not by a stretch
evidence: This claim is supported by MD simulations and electrophysiological experiments described in the results section.

claim: A number of hydrogen bonds along the force convey pathway are important for the mechanosensitivity of NompC.
source: a number of hydrogen bonds along the force convey pathway are important for the mechanosensitivity
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments and MD simulations showing loss of function when these hydrogen bonds are disrupted.

claim: Under intracellular compression, the bundled ankyrin repeat region acts like a spring with a spring constant of ~13 pN nm−1.
source: Under intracellular compression, the bundled ankyrin repeat region acts like a spring with a spring constant of ~13 pN nm−1
evidence: This is calculated from MD simulations as described in the results section.

claim: Forces are transferred through the ankyrin repeat region at a rate of ~1.8 nm ps−1.
source: by transferring forces at a rate of ~1.8 nm ps−1
evidence: This is calculated from MD simulations analyzing force propagation speed.

claim: The linker helix region acts as a bridge between the ankyrin repeats and the TRP domain.
source: The linker helix region acts as a bridge between the ankyrin repeats and the transient receptor potential (TRP) domain
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and confirmed by MD simulations.

claim: The pushing force is passed to the TRP domain to undergo a clockwise rotation, resulting in the opening of the channel.
source: which passes on the pushing force to the TRP domain to undergo a clockwise rotation, resulting in the opening of the channel
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations and PCA analysis showing conformational changes.

claim: This could be the universal gating mechanism of similar tethered mechanosensitive TRP channels.
source: This could be the universal gating mechanism of similar tethered mechanosensitive TRP channels
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings for NompC.

claim: The push-to-open mechanism enables cells to feel compression and shrinkage.
source: which enable cells to feel compression and shrinkage
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental and simulation results showing activation under compression.

claim: NompC is one of the earliest identified mechanosensitive ion channels belonging to the TRP family.
source: NompC is one of the earliest identified mechanosensitive ion channels belonging to the TRP family, which plays crucial roles in the sensation of light touch, hearing, balance, and locomotion of Drosophila melanogaster (Walker et al., 2000; Göpfert et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Zanini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: NompC plays crucial roles in the sensation of light touch, hearing, balance, and locomotion of Drosophila melanogaster.
source: which plays crucial roles in the sensation of light touch, hearing, balance, and locomotion of Drosophila melanogaster (Walker et al., 2000; Göpfert et al., 2006; Yan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Zanini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: NompC has 29 ankyrin repeats, the largest number among known TRP channels.
source: NompC is structurally unique as it has the largest number of ankyrin repeats (ARs) among the known TRP channels (Montell, 2005), 29 in total.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: The AR region is associated with microtubules.
source: The AR region is associated with microtubules, and it has been proposed to act as a gating spring to regulate the channel gating according to the so-called 'tethered gating model' (Albert et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2010b; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The AR region has been proposed to act as a gating spring to regulate channel gating according to the 'tethered gating model'.
source: it has been proposed to act as a gating spring to regulate the channel gating according to the so-called 'tethered gating model' (Albert et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2010b; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NompC orthologs have not been found in mammals.
source: Although NompC orthologs have not been found in mammals (Venkatachalam and Montell, 2007; Knecht et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NompC functions in mechanosensation of Caenorhabditis elegans and Danio rerio.
source: it was shown to function in mechanosensation of Caenorhabditis elegans and Danio rerio as well (Kang et al., 2010; Sidi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of NompC shows that four AR chains form an ~15-nm-long supercoiled helix.
source: The cryo-EM structure of NompC has been resolved (Jin et al., 2017), showing that four AR chains form an ~15-nm-long supercoiled helix and connect to the transmembrane (TM) pore domain via a linker helix (LH) region
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure cited.

claim: The four AR chains connect to the transmembrane pore domain via a linker helix region.
source: showing that four AR chains form an ~15-nm-long supercoiled helix and connect to the transmembrane (TM) pore domain via a linker helix (LH) region (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The channel remains closed throughout simulations without external forces.
source: We observed that the channel remains closed (with a very narrow constriction site, radius <1.0 Å, around the residue I1554) throughout the simulations without any external forces (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Video 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: The closed-state cryo-EM structure was stable in force-free MD simulations.
source: indicating that the closed-state cryo-EM structure was stable in our 'force-free' MD simulations.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability observed in MD simulations.

claim: When a pulling force is applied away from the membrane surface, the TM channel remains closed.
source: When the direction of the pulling force was away from the membrane surface, the TM channel also remained closed in our MD simulations (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Under pulling force, the channel was actually more closed than the free NompC.
source: In fact, the narrow region with a radius of less than 1 Å expanded in the latter part of the trajectory compared to the 'force-free' simulations, indicating that the channel was actually more closed than the free NompC in our 'pulling' simulations.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of MD simulation trajectories.

claim: When applying a pushing force toward the membrane on AR29, the narrowest constriction site of the channel was significantly dilated.
source: In contrast, when applying a proper pushing force (toward the membrane) on the AR29, we observed that the narrowest constriction site of the channel was significantly dilated in the latter part of the 'pushing' simulation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: The pore dilation was due to the global conformational change of the backbone rather than merely a side-chain movement.
source: We also conducted pore radius analysis based only on the backbone structures, and we observed the same trend as mentioned above (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), which confirmed that the pore dilation was due to the global conformational change of the backbone rather than merely a side-chain movement.
evidence: This is confirmed by additional analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The number of water molecules at the gate region increased in the pushing simulations compared to free and pulling simulations.
source: Our analysis showed that the number of water molecules was indeed evidently increased in the 'pushing' simulations, as compared to the 'free' and 'pulling' simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MD simulation data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Two spontaneous ion permeation events were observed only when the pore was dilated under a pushing force in the absence of TM potential.
source: In the absence of TM potential, we observed two spontaneous ion permeation events only when the pore was dilated under a pushing force (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Continuous ion permeation through the dilated pore was observed when applying a membrane potential of ±300 mV under pushing force.
source: When applying a membrane potential of ±300 mV, we observed continuous ion permeation through the dilated pore caused by the pushing force in our MD simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 7 and 8, Video 2).
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations shown in supplementary figures.

claim: NompC-expressed S2 cells showed a clear electrical signal under positive pressure in cell-attached patch-clamp experiments.
source: we detected a clear electrical signal through the NompC-expressed S2 cells under positive pressure, whereas the signal under negative pressure was nearly negligible.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Reference S2 cells without NompC showed no response to positive and negative pressure stimuli.
source: the reference Drosophila S2 cells without NompC expressed showed no response to the positive and negative pressure stimuli
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: A clear signal was detected through NompC-expressed S2 cells from outside-out patch clamp under negative pressure.
source: Similarly, we can detect a clear signal through the NompC-expressed S2 cells from the outside-out patch clamp under negative pressure which corresponds to the cell-attached patch clamp under positive pressure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: The signal under inside-out patch clamp with negative pressure was nearly negligible.
source: On the other hand, the signal under inside-out patch clamp with negative pressure was nearly negligible (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Electrical signals from cell-attached and outside-out patch clamp were nearly completely abolished after adding GdCl3.
source: The electrical signals from cell-attached patch clamp under positive pressure and outside-out patch clamp under negative pressure were nearly completely abolished after adding GdCl3 (a blocker for NompC) to the bath (Figure 1—figure supplement 10), confirming that the detected signal was indeed due to the ion permeation through NompC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments with blocker shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The second PCA eigenvector can distinguish the conformations of the free, pushing, and pulling simulations.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, the second PCA eigenvector can distinguish the conformations of the free, pushing, and pulling simulations very well, with the larger values corresponding to the more dilated states.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A clockwise rotation of the TRP domain was observed when a pushing force was applied to AR29.
source: We observed an evident clockwise rotation (looking from the intracellular side, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2, and Video 3) and an obvious upward tilt (looking from lateral side of membrane, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2, and Video 4) of the TRP domain when a pushing force was applied to the AR29.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MD simulation trajectories shown in figures.

claim: An upward tilt of the TRP domain was observed when a pushing force was applied to AR29.
source: We observed an evident clockwise rotation (looking from the intracellular side, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2, and Video 3) and an obvious upward tilt (looking from lateral side of membrane, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2, and Video 4) of the TRP domain when a pushing force was applied to the AR29.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MD simulation trajectories shown in figures.

claim: Clockwise rotation and upward tilt of the TRP domain may be associated with the opening of TRP channels.
source: This clockwise rotation and upward tilt of the TRP domain may be associated with the opening of the TRP channels (Liao et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Zheng and Qin, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous structural studies cited.

claim: The clockwise rotation of the TRP domain induced the S6 helices to rotate clockwise as well.
source: The overlaid structures in Figure 2B show that the clockwise rotation of the TRP domain induced the S6 helices (which are directly linked to the TRP domain) to rotate clockwise as well, albeit to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The gating constriction site is located at I1554 of the S6 helix.
source: The gating constriction site is located at I1554 of the S6 helix (Jin et al., 2017)
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure cited.

claim: I1554 residues were pulled away from the channel axis when the S6 helices rotate clockwise, leading to pore dilation.
source: and in our simulations, they were pulled away from the channel axis when the S6 helices rotate clockwise together with the TRP domain, leading to the dilation of the pore (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MD simulation trajectories shown in figures.

claim: Four stable hydrogen bonds were identified throughout the MD simulations around the TRP domain.
source: We analyzed the hydrogen bonding network around the TRP domain, and we attempted to locate the key residues ensuring the clockwise rotation of the TRP domain in response to the pushing force from AR. We identified four stable hydrogen bonds throughout the MD simulations (Figure 2D and E and Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is identified from analysis of MD simulation trajectories.

claim: Three of the four hydrogen bonds can be directly identified in the cryo-EM structure.
source: Three of the four hydrogen bonds can also be directly identified in the cryo-EM structure, except for the one between Q1253 and S1577, which was more stable only in the presence of a pushing force in the MD simulations (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is determined by comparing MD simulations with the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The hydrogen bond between Q1253 and S1577 was more stable only in the presence of a pushing force in MD simulations.
source: except for the one between Q1253 and S1577, which was more stable only in the presence of a pushing force in the MD simulations (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations.

claim: The W1572A mutation completely abolished the gating behavior of the channel.
source: In particular, the W1572A mutation completely abolished the gating behavior of the channel, consistent with the work of Jin et al., 2017.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: W1572 may be the rotation pivot of the TRP domain in MD trajectories.
source: Interestingly, we found that W1572 may be the rotation pivot of the TRP domain in our MD trajectory, which forms a stable hydrogen bond with the backbone of S1421 on the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of MD simulation trajectories.

claim: W1572 forms a stable hydrogen bond with the backbone of S1421 on the S4-S5 linker.
source: which forms a stable hydrogen bond with the backbone of S1421 on the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations.

claim: The S1421A mutation did not lead to significant loss-of-function of NompC.
source: Notably, this hydrogen bond does not involve the side chain of S1421, so the mutations at S1421 would not be expected to alter the above hydrogen bond and would not lead to significant loss-of-function of NompC. This was confirmed for S1421A, as shown by the dashed line in Figure 2F.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mutations S1577A, R1581A, K1244A, and Q1253A resulted in significant loss-of-function.
source: In addition, the mutations S1577A and R1581A on the TRP domain, and K1244A and Q1253A on the LH domain, all resulted in significant loss-of-function
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Five out of seven residues whose side chains form hydrogen bonds between the TRP and LH domains were crucial for proper gating behavior.
source: Thus, five out of seven residues, whose side chains form hydrogen bonds between the TRP and LH domains bonds as identified in our MD simulations, were crucial for the proper gating behavior of the NompC channel.
evidence: This is concluded from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: D1236 and E1571 were found to be replaceable by adjacent residues in stabilizing the local conformation.
source: The other two residues, D1236 and E1571, which are also involved in the hydrogen bonding between the TRP and LH domains, were found to be replaceable by adjacent residues in stabilizing the local conformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in supplementary figure.

claim: When pushing the four AR1 toward the membrane with a total force of 20 pN, the four AR29 apply a total torque of ~13 pN·nm on the LH domain pointing to the extracellular side.
source: The analysis indicated that when pushing the four AR1 toward the membrane with a total force of 20 pN (5 pN of force on each chain), the four AR29 apply a total torque of ~13 pN·nm on the LH domain pointing to the extracellular side, in addition to a dominant pushing force.
evidence: This is calculated from MD simulations.

claim: The torque applied by AR29 would help to rotate the TRP domain clockwise and drive the channel to open.
source: This torque would help to rotate the TRP domain clockwise and drive the channel to open (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of MD simulations shown in figures.

claim: The spring constant of each AR helix was estimated to be 3.3 ± 0.9 pN nm−1 in the supercoiled helix bundle.
source: The spring constant of each AR helix was estimated to be 3.3 ± 0.9 pN nm−1 in the supercoiled helix bundle formed by the four AR chains.
evidence: This is calculated from MD simulations.

claim: The whole AR helix bundle has a force constant of ~13 pN nm−1.
source: Thus, the whole AR helix bundle has a force constant of ~13 pN nm−1.
evidence: This is calculated from MD simulations.

claim: Previous atomic force microscopy measurements determined a force constant of 1.87 ± 0.31 pN nm−1 for a single AR chain.
source: For comparison, previous atomic force microscopy measurements determined a force constant of 1.87 ± 0.31 pN nm−1 for a single AR chain (Lee et al., 2006)
evidence: This is cited from previous experimental work.

claim: Previous steered MD simulations obtained a force constant value of ~4.0 pN nm−1 for a single AR chain.
source: and previous steered MD (SMD) simulations obtained a value of ~4.0 pN nm−1 (Sotomayor et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous simulation work.

claim: SMD on a single 29-AR spring estimated the spring constant to be 2.5 ± 0.4 pN nm−1.
source: For comparison, we performed SMD on a single 29-AR spring and estimated the spring constant to be 2.5 ± 0.4 pN nm−1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is calculated from SMD simulations shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The four AR helices are not tightly coupled.
source: The close agreement of the values from the single AR and one AR in the supercoiled complex indicated that the four AR helices are not tightly coupled.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of simulation results.

claim: The AR supercoiled spring remained in its elastic limits in the study.
source: Therefore, the AR supercoiled spring remained in its elastic limits in the study, although in the SMD trajectories with larger forces, the ARs showed a degree of distortion (Video 5).
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of simulations with varying forces.

claim: The deviation of the directions of forces exerted on the LH regions occurred after about 7-8 ps when the AR region was stretched or compressed.
source: The deviation of the directions of the forces exerted on the LH regions when the AR region was stretched or compressed occurred after about 7-8 ps (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is calculated from MD simulations shown in figures.

claim: The force was transferred through the AR region at a speed of 1.8 ± 0.2 nm ps−1.
source: Considering that the length of the relaxed AR region is about 15 nm, we estimated that the force was transferred through the AR region at a speed of 1.8 ± 0.2 nm ps−1.
evidence: This is calculated from MD simulations.

claim: Forces are propagated via membranes at a speed of 1.4 ± 0.5 nm ps−1.
source: A recent study showed that forces are propagated via membranes at a speed of 1.4 ± 0.5 nm ps−1 (Aponte-Santamaría et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The force transfer speed in the tethered NompC channel is comparable to, or slightly faster than, that in membranes.
source: Therefore, it appears that the force transfer speed in the tethered NompC channel is comparable to, or slightly faster, than that in the membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with cited work.

claim: Two stable hydrogen bonds were found between the ARs and LHs in MD trajectories, between W1115 and D1142, and R1127 and E1163.
source: We also found two stable hydrogen bonds between the ARs and LHs in the MD trajectories, between W1115 and D1142, and R1127 and E1163, respectively (Figure 3E and Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is identified from MD simulations shown in figure.

claim: Mutations D1142A, R1127A, and E1163A led to significant loss-of-function in electrophysiology experiments.
source: Mutations of D1142A, R1127A, and E1163A, which break the hydrogen bonds but show normal membrane targeting, led to a significant loss-of-function in the electrophysiology experiment (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in figures.

claim: W1115A does little to alter the mechanosensing behavior.
source: However, W1115A does little to alter the mechanosensing behavior (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological experiments shown in figures.

claim: The role of W1115 can be replaced by the adjacent Y1109, which can form a stable hydrogen bond with D1142 in the presence of the W1115A mutation.
source: probably because its hydrogen bonding and stabilizing role can be replaced by the adjacent Y1109, which can form a stable hydrogen bond with D1142 in the presence of the W1115A mutation as observed in our MD simulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The interface between the AR and LH regions is crucial for force transduction.
source: These results indicate that the interface between the AR and LH regions is crucial for the force transduction, further supporting the tethered spring model for NompC.
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Compression or shrinkage of cells can compress the AR spring, generating a pushing force and a torque on the TRP domain.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4, compression or shrinkage of cells can compress the AR spring, which generates a pushing force and also a torque on the TRP domain with a component pointing to the extracellular side and perpendicular to the membrane surface.
evidence: This is illustrated based on the findings from simulations and experiments.

claim: The torque is generated by the specific supercoiled structure of the AR region.
source: The torque is generated by the specific supercoiled structure of the AR region, as demonstrated by the mechanics study of Argudo et al., 2019.
evidence: This is supported by a cited mechanics study.

claim: The pushing force alone may be sufficient to generate a clockwise motion of the TRP domain.
source: Our simulations indicate that the pushing force alone may be sufficient to generate a clockwise motion of the TRP domain, which in turn pulls the S6 helices to open the NompC gate.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulations.

claim: Critical residues R1581, W1572, Q1253, S1577, and K1244 ensure that the TRP domain will rotate clockwise around the pivot W1572 when a pushing force is applied to the LH region.
source: Critical residues between the TRP domain and LH, including R1581, W1572, Q1253, S1577, and K1244, as well as the presence of the S4-S5 linker above the TRP domain, ensure that the TRP domain will rotate clockwise around the pivot W1572 when a pushing force is applied to the LH region.
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis experiments and MD simulations.

claim: A TRPV1 mutant with only two ARs can be mechanically opened by a pushing force.
source: This is consistent with a study showing that a TRPV1 mutant, which has only two ARs, can be mechanically opened by a pushing force (Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: TRP channels similar to NompC with a certain number of ARs can be tethered to microtubules and use the push-to-open mechanism to sense and respond to cell shrinkage or compression.
source: We believe that TRP channels similar to NompC, with a certain number of ARs, can be tethered to microtubules and use the push (-AR)-to-open mechanism to sense and respond to cell shrinkage or compression.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings for NompC.

claim: The push-to-open sensing mechanism can be complementary to the stretch-to-open mechanism that responds to cell expansion.
source: This sensing mechanism can be complementary to the well-studied stretch(-membrane)-to-open mechanism that responds to cell expansion.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings and comparison with known mechanisms.

claim: A stable lipid molecule has been found near H1423 in the cryo-EM map.
source: Previous studies showed that lipid molecules may be involved in NompC gating and a stable lipid molecule has been found near H1423 in the cryo-EM map (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from the cryo-EM structure study.

claim: H1423 can stably interact with a POPC lipid molecule in MD simulations.
source: Our analysis on MD simulation trajectories also showed that H1423 can stably interact with a 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC) lipid molecule.
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations.

claim: A POPC lipid molecule rapidly diffused to a location similar to that in the cryo-EM structure and acted as a bridge to link H1423 and S1268.
source: This lipid molecule was not in the interacting pocket in the initial simulation system but rapidly diffused to a location similar to that in the cryo-EM structure and acted as a bridge to link H1423 and S1268 (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations shown in figures.

claim: Lipid molecules can help stabilize the local structure of NompC around H1423 and/or convey forces from the membrane.
source: This suggested that lipid molecules can help stabilize the local structure of NompC around H1423 and/or convey forces from the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation observations.

claim: The addition of OAG to the intracellular monolayer tends to activate NompC.
source: The experiments showed that the addition of OAG to the intracellular monolayer tends to activate NompC, while adding OAG to the extracellular monolayer had the opposite effect (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch-clamping recordings shown in figures.

claim: Adding OAG to the extracellular monolayer had the opposite effect on NompC activation.
source: while adding OAG to the extracellular monolayer had the opposite effect (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by patch-clamping recordings shown in figures.

claim: The OAG-induced activation finding was consistent with previous studies on TRPC6.
source: This finding was consistent with previous studies on TRPC6 (Nikolaev et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The unidirectional OAG-induced activation suggests a synergetic gating mechanism.
source: The unidirectional OAG-induced activation suggests a synergetic gating mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Pushing the AR spring would lead to intrinsic gating of NompC and could simultaneously generate a membrane curvature and an asymmetrical stress profile that may also facilitate channel gating.
source: Pushing the AR spring would lead to the intrinsic gating of NompC and could simultaneously generate a membrane curvature and an asymmetrical stress profile that may also facilitate the channel gating.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The ion conductance in the MD simulations was smaller than the experimental results for the fully open state due to limitations of the simulation timescale.
source: Due to limitations of the simulation timescale, we were unable to observe the full gating process of the NompC. Therefore, the ion conductance in the MD simulations was smaller than the experimental results for the fully open state.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation of the MD simulations.

claim: A clear and detailed opening trend of the channel in the presence of pushing forces was seen in the MD simulations and supported by electrophysiological experiments.
source: Nonetheless, a clear and detailed opening trend of the channel in the presence of pushing forces was seen in the MD simulations and this was supported by electrophysiological experiments.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of simulation and experimental results.
